HyperCom Overview

library(HyperCom)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(ggplot2)

Load in example data

HyperCom requires three inputs:

  1. A dense gene x cell matrix with genes as row names and cells as column names

  2. A dataframe of cell metadata containing sample and optionally group columns which need to be specified as variables

  3. A dataframe of ligand-receptor (LR) interactions where each gene in an interaction has its own column

  • HyperCom contains the correctly formatted CellChat database for human and mouse which can be accessed via the cellchat.hs.lrdb and cellchat.mm.lrdb respectively.

In this vignette we will use a 1000 cell subset of heart failure from Alexanian et al, 2021.

counts <- readRDS("alexanian2021.counts.rds")
dim(counts)
#> [1] 17083  1000
head(rownames(counts))
#> [1] "Xkr4"   "Sox17"  "Mrpl15" "Lypla1" "Tcea1"  "Rgs20"
head(colnames(counts))
#> [1] "AACCGCGTCCAGAGGA-2" "AACTCAGCACGAGGTA-2" "AACTCTTGTGCGAAAC-2"
#> [4] "AAGGAGCAGGATCGCA-2" "ACACCAAAGACCCACC-2" "ACACCGGAGCTACCGC-2"
meta.data <- read.csv("alexanian2021.metadata.csv", row.names = 1)
sample.column <- "sample"
group.column <- "condition"
head(meta.data)
#>                    sample condition    celltype     UMAP_1     UMAP_2
#> AACCGCGTCCAGAGGA-2      2      SHAM Endothelial  1.2676813 -10.036637
#> AACTCAGCACGAGGTA-2      2      SHAM Endothelial  1.7707077  -9.448688
#> AACTCTTGTGCGAAAC-2      2      SHAM Endothelial  0.2925013  -9.781118
#> AAGGAGCAGGATCGCA-2      2      SHAM Endothelial  1.1058826 -10.454998
#> ACACCAAAGACCCACC-2      2      SHAM Endothelial -3.3748763 -10.034042
#> ACACCGGAGCTACCGC-2      2      SHAM Endothelial  3.9700553  -8.899605
ggplot(meta.data, aes(x=UMAP_1, y=UMAP_2, colour=celltype)) +
  geom_point(size=0.5) +
  theme_classic()

For the LR interactions we will use the CellChat murine database.

lrdb <- cellchat.mm.lrdb
dim(lrdb)
#> [1] 2377    6
head(lrdb)
#>                 edges ligand     r1     r2   r3   r4
#> 1 TGFB1_TGFBR1_TGFBR2  Tgfb1 Tgfbr1 Tgfbr2 <NA> <NA>
#> 2 TGFB2_TGFBR1_TGFBR2  Tgfb2 Tgfbr1 Tgfbr2 <NA> <NA>
#> 3 TGFB3_TGFBR1_TGFBR2  Tgfb3 Tgfbr1 Tgfbr2 <NA> <NA>
#> 4 TGFB1_ACVR1B_TGFBR2  Tgfb1 Acvr1b Tgfbr2 <NA> <NA>
#> 5 TGFB1_ACVR1C_TGFBR2  Tgfb1 Acvr1c Tgfbr2 <NA> <NA>
#> 6 TGFB2_ACVR1B_TGFBR2  Tgfb2 Acvr1b Tgfbr2 <NA> <NA>

Running HyperCom

Preprocessing

In order to reduce memory usage, we first filter the counts matrix to only genes present in the LR interactions with expression greater than 0. The function also transposes the matrix.

lr.counts <- filter_counts(counts=counts, lrdb=lrdb, outfile=NULL)
dim(lr.counts)
#> [1] 1000  663

Next we filter the ligand receptor interactions to only interactions where all genes are present in the filtered expression matrix.

lrs <- generate_lrs_table(counts=lr.counts, lrdb=lrdb, outfile=NULL)
dim(lrs)
#> [1] 1042    5

Generating Hypergraph

To generate the hyperedges, which are edges that contain multiple nodes, we use the expression matrix LR interaction to create 3 types of hyperedges:

  1. expression edges - edges containing cells that express a given ligand or receptor

  2. complex edges - edges containing the genes that comprise a receptor complex

  3. interaction edges - edges containing the genes that comprise an LR interaction

HyperCom represents these hyperedges as a dataframe with an edge and node column where the node belongs to the edge. The weight is set to 1 for each edge.

hyperedgelist <- generate_hyperedges(counts=lr.counts, lrs=lrs, outfile=NULL)
head(hyperedgelist)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   edges               nodes  weight
#>   <chr>               <chr>   <dbl>
#> 1 TGFB1_TGFBR1_TGFBR2 Tgfb1       1
#> 2 TGFB1_TGFBR1_TGFBR2 Tgfbr1      1
#> 3 TGFB1_TGFBR1_TGFBR2 Tgfbr2      1
#> 4 TGFB2_TGFBR1_TGFBR2 Tgfb2       1
#> 5 TGFB2_TGFBR1_TGFBR2 Tgfbr1      1
#> 6 TGFB2_TGFBR1_TGFBR2 Tgfbr2      1

We can represent this hypergraph as an adjacency matrix where the nodes are the cells, ligand genes, and receptor genes. Each entry is the number hyperedges shared by nodes.

adj <- generate_adjacency_matrix(hyperedgelist=hyperedgelist, outfile=NULL)
dim(adj)
#> [1] 1663 1663

Calculating Network Connectivity

In order to calculate the network connectivity of the hypergraph we perform a random walk on the adjacency matrix to produce an influence matrix.

infMat <- calculate_infMat(adj=adj, outfile=NULL)
dim(infMat)
#> [1] 1663 1663

Downstream Analysis

To account for genes now being present in the matrices, we then process the metadata to contain information on the genes as well as cell metadata. Additionally to reduce memory, we reduce the number of columns to just node, sample, and group.

metadata <- generate_metadata(infMat=infMat, metadata=meta.data, sample=sample.column, group=group.column, outfile=NULL)
head(metadata)
#>                 cell sample group
#> 1 AAAGATGCACAGATTC-3      3   TAC
#> 2 AAAGATGCAGCTCGCA-3      3   TAC
#> 3 AAAGATGCAGGTCTCG-3      3   TAC
#> 4 AAAGATGGTGTTTGGT-2      2  SHAM
#> 5 AAAGTAGAGGAGTTTA-2      2  SHAM
#> 6 AAAGTAGCACATTTCT-2      2  SHAM

Scoring Network Activity

We can score network activity using the influence matrix to understand globally if cells are sending or receiving signals. HyperCom scoring generates a sender and receiver score based on a given matrix and uses both to create a composite HyperCom score. This HyperCom score ranges from -1 to 1 going from better senders to better receivers.

network.score <- score_hypercom(infMat=infMat, metadata=metadata)
head(network.score)
#>                 cell    sender  receiver       dif       avg  hypercom
#> 1 GGGACCTGTGGGTATG-3 0.5554141 0.9671508 0.4117368 0.7612825 0.7368970
#> 2 GCTTCCAAGCCTCGTG-3 0.5386332 0.9659989 0.4273656 0.7523160 0.7327363
#> 3 CATTATCTCCGCTGTT-3 0.4904711 0.9646571 0.4741860 0.7275641 0.7239227
#> 4 ACACTGAGTTGTGGCC-3 0.5680951 0.9575791 0.3894840 0.7628371 0.7238935
#> 5 CCATGTCCACAGGCCT-3 0.5206136 0.9546570 0.4340433 0.7376353 0.7236062
#> 6 ACGAGCCAGAGGTTGC-2 0.4856558 0.9585472 0.4728914 0.7221015 0.7170417

Here we can see that globally, communication is higher in TAC.

meta.data$cell <- rownames(meta.data)
network.score <- left_join(network.score, meta.data, by=join_by(cell))

transparent <- rgb(255, 255, 255, max=255, alpha = 0)
ggplot(network.score, aes(x=UMAP_1, y=UMAP_2, colour=hypercom)) +
  geom_point(size=0.5) +
  scale_color_gradient2(low="blue", mid=transparent, high="red", limits=c(-1,1)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(condition)) +
  theme_classic()

Identifying Important LR Pairs

We can also identify important LR pairs by using HyperCom scoring on LR pairs. This prioritization scores LR pairs to find highly communicative LR pairs that are optionally group specific. The prioritize_lr function can be run sequentially or parallelly. The parallel implementation uses the parallelly package.

priority <- prioritize_lr(lrs=lrs, adj=adj, infMat=infMat, metadata=metadata, parallel=TRUE, outfile=NULL)
head(priority)
#>               edges ligand    r1    r2   r3  priority
#> 1        THBS1_SDC4  Thbs1  Sdc4  <NA> <NA> 0.3307897
#> 2        PGF_VEGFR1    Pgf  Flt1  <NA> <NA> 0.3173039
#> 3         COMP_SDC4   Comp  Sdc4  <NA> <NA> 0.2917878
#> 4 POSTN_ITGAV_ITGB5  Postn Itgav Itgb5 <NA> 0.2915502
#> 5          FN1_SDC4    Fn1  Sdc4  <NA> <NA> 0.2711980
#> 6          FN1_CD44    Fn1  Cd44  <NA> <NA> 0.2691572

We see that Thbs1 Sdc4 is the highest scoring LR pair. We can calculate HyperCom scores for this pair. As a note, the score_hypercom function can also take a vector of receptor genes if the receptor is a complex.

Thbs1_Sdc4 <- score_hypercom(infMat=infMat, metadata=metadata, ligand="Thbs1", receptors="Sdc4")
head(Thbs1_Sdc4)
#>                 cell    sender  receiver       dif       avg  hypercom
#> 1 ATTATCCAGCTACCGC-3 0.4555440 0.9485435 0.4929995 0.7020437 0.6893943
#> 2 ACTGTCCCAATAACGA-2 0.4912161 0.9117634 0.4205473 0.7014897 0.6312705
#> 3 CGTTAGAGTTACGCGC-3 0.4744556 0.8981270 0.4236714 0.6862913 0.6244633
#> 4 CTGAAGTAGTCGTTTG-3 0.4051788 0.8627810 0.4576022 0.6339799 0.6079607
#> 5 CCCAGTTTCATGCTCC-3 0.3959453 0.8545903 0.4586450 0.6252678 0.6008580
#> 6 AGGTCCGGTGTTGGGA-2 0.5717083 0.9045992 0.3328908 0.7381538 0.5999808

If we plot the sender and receiver score we see both higher densities of sender and receiver cells in TAC.

Thbs1_Sdc4 <- left_join(Thbs1_Sdc4, metadata, by=join_by(cell))
ggplot(Thbs1_Sdc4, aes(x=sender, y=receiver, colour=group)) +
  geom_density_2d() +
  theme_classic()

Side Note: Communication Clusters

Although clustering is not necessary for any step in HyperCom, it may be useful to conceptualize how groups of cells are communicating. We can cluster the influence matrix to generate communication clusters. Here we use Seurat’s implementation of Louvain clustering.

library(Seurat)
#> Loading required package: SeuratObject
#> Loading required package: sp
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'SeuratObject'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, t
generate_com_clusters <- function(infMat, metadata){
  com.seurat <- CreateSeuratObject(t(infMat), meta.data = metadata, project="communication")
  com.seurat <- NormalizeData(com.seurat, verbose=FALSE)
  com.seurat <- FindVariableFeatures(com.seurat, selection.method = "vst", nfeatures = 2000, verbose=FALSE)
  all.genes <- rownames(com.seurat)
  com.seurat <- ScaleData(com.seurat, features = all.genes, verbose=FALSE)
  com.seurat <- RunPCA(com.seurat, features = VariableFeatures(object = com.seurat), verbose=FALSE)
  com.seurat <- FindNeighbors(com.seurat, dims = 1:10, verbose=FALSE)
  com.seurat <- FindClusters(com.seurat, resolution = 0.5, cluster.name = "com_clusters", verbose=FALSE)
  com.seurat <- RunUMAP(com.seurat, dims = 1:10, verbose=FALSE)
  
  hyper.com_clusters <- dplyr::select(com.seurat@meta.data, cell, com_clusters)
  metadata <- left_join(metadata, hyper.com_clusters, by=join_by(cell))
  metadata$com_clusters <- factor(metadata$com_clusters)
  
  return(metadata)
}

We can see that communication clusters do not necessarily line up with the annotated cell types.

com_clusters <- generate_com_clusters(infMat=infMat, metadata=metadata)
#> Warning: Data is of class matrix. Coercing to dgCMatrix.
#> Warning: The default method for RunUMAP has changed from calling Python UMAP via reticulate to the R-native UWOT using the cosine metric
#> To use Python UMAP via reticulate, set umap.method to 'umap-learn' and metric to 'correlation'
#> This message will be shown once per session

annotations <- select(meta.data, celltype)
annotations$cell <- rownames(annotations)
com_clusters <- left_join(com_clusters, annotations, by=join_by(cell))
com_clusters <- filter(com_clusters, group != "gene")

ggplot(com_clusters, aes(x=com_clusters, fill=celltype)) +
  geom_bar() +
  theme_classic()
